newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: One body found in Australia ski resort ruins.
newsitem.headline: One body found in Australia ski resort ruins.

text.p: One body was found on Thursday in the ruins of two Australian ski lodges destroyed in a landslide and police said a search was continuing for up to 20 people believed to be buried in the ruins.
"Fairly recently we have found one body," regional police commander Bruce Johnston told reporters as rescuers continued searching under arc lights for survivors in the freezing night.
Police said the body was still in the ruins of the ski lodges and that they could not identify it.
"I think you might find there would be more bodies found tonight," senior constable Scott Willis later told reporters.

Police had earlier said that rescuers using optic fibre cameras and thermal imaging had found no signs of life in the ruins of the Thredbo Alpine Village in the Snowy Mountains, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.
Darkness had fallen and temperatures plummeted below freezing as the search entered its 19th hour. "The longer we go the more our hopes are diminishing," Johnston said.
The landslide hit just before midnight on Wednesday, sending tonnes of soil, rocks and gum trees crashing into the Carinya lodge, which contained one person.
It then cascaded onto the Bimbadeen lodge, which contained up to 19 people, including Americans.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard, in hospital in Sydney where he is recovering from pneumonia, sent a message of support to the families of those trapped in the rubble and to rescuers.
"The thoughts and prayers of the entire nation are with those people unaccounted for and their families and friends following the Thredbo tragedy," Howard said in a statement.
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said in Tokyo he will cut short a visit to Japan because of the landslide and that he would visit the area at the appropriate time.
"I think the priority is the rescue effort," Fischer told reporters. "The state emergency services, the police, and, if the need arises, the defence forces are there."

In Thredbo, rescuers were unable to launch an immediate full-scale search for survivors because the site was dangerously unstable, with more landslides feared, police said. Witnesses had reported hearing cries for help shortly after the landslide.
"There were cries that were heard very soon after the slippage, but nothing has been heard since," Johnston said.
Light snow dusted a human chain of rescuers who sifted by hand through the twisted ruins of the lodges, unable to use earth moving equipment for fear of more landslides.
Witnesses said the landslide sounded like a big gust of wind that shook the lodges perched on the side of the mountain.
"We just heard this enormous rush like I'd imagine you'd experience with a tornado just hitting a building...," said Glenn Milne, who was holidaying in an adjacent lodge.

Milne said he joined other nearby residents in trying to claw away rubble as anti-theft alarms from buried cars sounded from beneath the wreckage immediately after the landslide. Other cars teetered precariously on top of the ruins.
The landslide occurred just before midnight at a time when Thredbo, at an altitude of 1,370 metres (4,494 feet), was packed with thousands of Australian and foreign visitors.
Thredbo sits on a ridge facing the snow-covered mountain range of the Kosciuszko National Park, which rises to 2,037 metres (6,683 feet).
Australia's ski season runs from June to October but has started slowly this year as little snow has fallen.

Police believe seepage from a mountain spring may have caused the earth to give way. Lodges further down the slope escaped the landslide, allowing rescuers easy road access to the scene and for evacuations.
"It looks like someone has taken a great big bulldozer and just drove over both the lodges and they just slid down the hill," one unidentified witness told reporters.
